1.title: Daily Scrum
1.text: Welcome to Module 8: Daily Scrum. Fifteen minutes a day, and more exam traps than almost any other event. In this module you will learn what the Daily Scrum is for, who it belongs to, how the Developers run it, and how it differs from a status meeting. That last point is a learning objective of its own.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. State the purpose, participants and timebox of the Daily Scrum. Explain how the Developers conduct one. Give three ways it differs from a status meeting. Explain why its constraints help the Developers. Say what the Scrum Master does, and does not do, there. And spot the traps: status reports, long talks, and mandatory questions.

1.title: Case Check-In: The Status Report
1.text: At RideLoop, the team meets at nine thirty in the operations room, every working day. Lately, Grace Whitfield has started to sit in, and Grace asks each Developer for a status report. The talk now runs twenty-five minutes, and the plan for the day gets lost. You are the Scrum Master, and you think about what this event is actually for. By the end of the module, you will know how to explain it to Grace.

1.title: Purpose, Participants and Rules
1.text: Here are the rules. The purpose: check progress toward the Sprint Goal, and adjust the Sprint Backlog and the coming work. It is for the Developers. It lasts fifteen minutes, at a fixed time and place each working day. The Product Owner and Scrum Master take part only as Developers, and only when they are working on Sprint Backlog items. The Developers choose the structure, but it must focus on the Sprint Goal and end with "an actionable plan for the next day of work."

1.title: Daily Scrum or Status Meeting?
1.text: The Daily Scrum is often confused with a status meeting, so look at the picture. The Daily Scrum is the Developers' own planning event, for themselves, toward the Sprint Goal. A status meeting is a report to someone who oversees the work. The room can be the same, and the clock can be the same, but the purpose is different. If an option turns the Daily Scrum into status reporting, it is wrong.

1.title: How the Developers Conduct a Daily Scrum
1.text: How do the Developers conduct one? The Guide leaves the format to them, so this slide shows a typical flow that satisfies its rules, and it goes beyond the Guide. Gather at the same time and place, in front of the Sprint Backlog. Inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal. Adapt the Sprint Backlog and the plan, but never the Sprint Goal. Plan the next day of work. Raise impediments. And close within fifteen minutes, moving deep conversations to a follow-up.

1.title: Ways to Structure It
1.text: There is more than one way to structure it. These formats go beyond the Guide, which leaves the structure to the Developers. Walk the board: go through the Sprint Backlog item by item. Work by Sprint Goal: ask what stands between the team and the goal today. Use free discussion about the plan, with discipline. Or use the three questions, an example only: what helped, what is next, and what blocks. The earlier edition of the Guide offered those three questions as an example. The current Guide removed them, and lets the Developers choose.

1.title: Not a Status Meeting
1.text: The learning objective asks for at least three differences from a status meeting. The comparison goes beyond the Guide, but each difference follows from it. Purpose: the Daily Scrum plans the next day toward the Sprint Goal, while a status meeting reports on past work. Whose event: the Developers', not a manager's. Direction: Developers talk to each other, rather than each person reporting up. Outcome: an actionable plan and an updated Sprint Backlog, not a report. And structure: chosen by the Developers, not by a manager. And focus: the Sprint Goal, not individual tasks and hours. That is six, and the objective asks for only three.

1.title: Why the Constraints Help
1.text: The constraints are not bureaucracy; they protect the Developers. Fifteen minutes keeps the event short and focused, and details come afterwards. The same time and place removes scheduling effort. Making it for the Developers gives them ownership and room for honest talk, with no reporting up. Focusing on the Sprint Goal keeps one objective in view. A plan for the next day turns inspection into adaptation. And choosing their own structure builds self-management.

1.title: The Plan Changes, the Goal Does Not
1.text: The Daily Scrum is the Developers' inspection point for the Sprint Backlog. What they adapt is the plan, never the Sprint Goal. If the work turns out different from what they expected, they negotiate scope with the Product Owner, without harming the Sprint Goal. Adaptation happens as soon as something new is learned. And the Developers can adjust the plan at other moments too: they often meet during the day for more detailed re-planning.

1.title: Who May Attend
1.text: Who takes part? The event belongs to the Developers. The Product Owner and Scrum Master take part only as Developers, when they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items. The Scrum Master makes sure the event happens and stays within fifteen minutes, but does not run it and does not collect status. Stakeholders and managers who want to know progress can see the Sprint Backlog and the Increment, and they come to the Sprint Review. At RideLoop, that is the answer for Grace: read the Sprint Backlog and come to the Review, but the Daily Scrum is not a report to Grace.

1.title: Common Problems and Better Practice
1.text: Common problems, with better practice; both go beyond the Guide. Everyone reports to the Scrum Master: the Developers should talk to each other about the plan. It runs past fifteen minutes: park deeper topics for a follow-up. The time and place keep changing: fix them. Nothing changes afterwards: end with a plan and an updated Sprint Backlog. Only yesterday is reported: look forward to today and tomorrow. And the Scrum Master runs it: instead, the Developers run it.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. The purpose is to plan toward the Sprint Goal, not to report status. Fifteen minutes, every working day, at the same time and place. It is the Developers' event, and the Product Owner and Scrum Master join only as Developers. The Developers choose the structure; the three questions are old. The Scrum Master does not run it or collect status. And the Sprint Goal does not change at the Daily Scrum; the plan does. The Guide adds that Daily Scrums improve communication, identify impediments and promote quick decisions, and so eliminate the need for other meetings. An extra status meeting goes against that.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. The Daily Scrum checks progress toward the Sprint Goal and adjusts the plan. It lasts fifteen minutes, at one fixed time and place, every working day. The Developers own it and choose the structure. The output is an actionable plan for the next day. It is not a status meeting. And the Scrum Master ensures it happens but does not run it. Now test yourself.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A discussion about a design problem makes the RideLoop Daily Scrum run to twenty-five minutes every day. What is the best action? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. The Daily Scrum stays at fifteen minutes, and the people concerned continue the discussion afterwards. The Developers often meet during the day for details. Extending the event or stopping it loses its purpose.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A new contractor tells the RideLoop team that every Daily Scrum must follow three questions: what did I do yesterday, what will I do today, and what is blocking me. What does the Guide say? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. The Developers choose the structure, as long as the event focuses on the Sprint Goal and produces a plan. The three questions were an example in the earlier edition.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. You, the Scrum Master, are also working on a Sprint Backlog item. Must you attend the Daily Scrum? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. A Scrum Master who is actively working on Sprint Backlog items takes part as a Developer. Otherwise the event belongs to the Developers, and the Scrum Master does not run it or collect status.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which statement is a difference between the Daily Scrum and a status meeting? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. The Daily Scrum is the Developers' own planning event, not a report to a manager. Option D reverses the two meetings, and option C gives the event to the Product Owner.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. What must the Daily Scrum focus on and produce? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D: progress toward the Sprint Goal, and a concrete plan for the next working day. Status reports, a review of the Increment, and the next Sprint's goal all belong elsewhere.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: B. Keep to fifteen minutes. Question two: A. The Developers choose the structure. Question three: C. A Scrum Master working on Sprint Backlog items takes part as a Developer. Question four: B. The Developers' own planning, not a report upward. Question five: D. Progress toward the Sprint Goal, and a plan. That completes Module 8. Next, Module 9 covers the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective.
